vocabulary.definition: A statistical question expects varied answers that can be collected as data.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una pregunta estadística espera respuestas variadas que se pueden recopilar como datos.
vocabulary.visual: How many minutes do students in our class read each night?
vocabulary.cloze: A question that expects varied answers you can collect is a ___ ___.

examples.text: “How tall is each student in my class?”
examples.why: Different students give different answers, so the data varies.
One person, one measurement — nothing varies.

vocabulary.definition: A question answered with data that are expected to vary.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una pregunta que se responde con datos que se espera que varíen.
vocabulary.visual: “How tall are the players on the team?” → answers vary: 60 in, 63 in, 58 in, 65 in
vocabulary.cloze: A question that expects a variety of answers and is answered by collecting data is a ___.

examples.text: How tall are the students in my class?
examples.why: The answers vary, so data must be collected.
It has one fixed answer, so it is not statistical.

vocabulary.definition: A question that does not anticipate variability in the data used to answer it. It may ask for one fact or measurement.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una pregunta que no anticipa variabilidad en los datos usados para responderla. Puede pedir un solo dato o una medición.
vocabulary.visual: “How tall am I?” → one answer: 60 in. Everyone who measures gets the same number.
vocabulary.cloze: A question that does not anticipate variability in the data is a ___.

examples.text: How many days are in a week?
examples.why: The answer is always 7 — it never varies, so there is no data to collect.

examples.text: How tall are the students in my class?
examples.why: Different students have different heights, so the answers vary — that makes it statistical.

vocabulary.definition: Facts and numbers you collect, like answers to a survey.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Datos y números que recoges, como respuestas a una encuesta.
vocabulary.visual: Player heights: 60 in, 63 in, 58 in, 65 in — four different measurements
vocabulary.cloze: Facts or numbers collected to answer a question are ___.

examples.text: The 20 quiz scores collected from the class
examples.why: Facts gathered from a group, ready to describe.
The instrument is not the information it produced.

vocabulary.definition: How spread out the numbers are.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Qué tan separados están los números.
vocabulary.visual: Scores 10, 12, 11 are close together (low variability); scores 2, 15, 30 are far apart (high variability)
vocabulary.cloze: How much the values in a data set differ from one another is the ___.

examples.why: The values differ, which is what variability measures.
Nothing varies, so there is no spread to describe.

vocabulary.definition: Collecting facts by asking people questions.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Recoger datos haciendo preguntas a las personas.
vocabulary.visual: Asking 50 students 'What is your favorite sport?' and recording the answers
vocabulary.cloze: A way to collect data by asking many people the same question is a ___.

examples.text: Asking every student how many minutes they read last night
examples.why: Facts collected by asking a group the same question.

examples.text: Looking up one fact in a book

vocabulary.definition: How the data looks: where it sits and how spread out it is.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Cómo se ven los datos: dónde están y qué tan separados están.
vocabulary.visual: A distribution is symmetric when its left and right sides have approximately matching shapes around the center.

vocabulary.definition: A number line with one dot for each data value.

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Surveys and Statistics
revealWordProblem.text: Some sixth-grade students want to get more food choices in the cafeteria. They will conduct a survey of students who buy lunch in the cafeteria. What questions should they include in their survey? Explain your choices.
revealWordProblem.imageAlt: A photo of a school lunch tray holding almonds, celery and carrot sticks, milk, an apple, and a sandwich.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: A good survey question must be a statistical question — one that anticipates variability, since different students will give different answers. Two strong choices: 'On a scale of 1 to 5, how satisfied are you with the current cafeteria food choices?' and 'Which new lunch item would you most like to see added: pizza, tacos, a salad bar, or stir-fry?' Both work because the answers will differ from student to student and can be tallied — for example, if 45 out of 80 students surveyed pick tacos, that's 45 ÷ 80 = 0.5625 = 56.25% of respondents, showing tacos as the clear favorite to petition for. A question like 'How many days a week does the cafeteria serve lunch?' would NOT belong on the survey, because it has one fixed answer for every student and doesn't anticipate variability.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a statistical question?
choices: How many points did each player score this season?
How many points are scored for a free throw?
What sport does this team play?
How many halves are in a soccer game?
questions.explanation: "How many points did each player score?" is statistical because different players will have different scores — there is variability in the data.
choiceFeedback: A free throw's points are fixed—does this question ask about variation?
What sport is played doesn't vary—do different people answer this differently?
Halves in a game is a rule—does it change from one observation to another?
hints: Re-read each question and ask: would different people or games give different answers, or is there just one fixed answer?
A statistical question expects variability — many answers that differ. Sort each choice into 'one fixed answer' or 'answers that vary'.
Test one: 'How many halves are in a soccer game?' Every game has the same number — no variability there. Check the other three the same way.
questions.stemEs: ¿Cuál de las siguientes es una pregunta estadística?
questions.explanationEs: «¿Cuántos puntos anotó cada jugador?» es estadística porque distintos jugadores tendrán puntajes distintos: hay variabilidad en los datos.
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer cada pregunta y pregunta: ¿personas o juegos distintos darían respuestas distintas, o hay una sola respuesta fija?
Una pregunta estadística espera variabilidad — muchas respuestas distintas. Clasifica cada opción en 'una sola respuesta fija' o 'respuestas que varían'.
Prueba una: '¿Cuántos tiempos hay en un partido de fútbol?' Todos los partidos tienen el mismo número — ahí no hay variabilidad. Revisa las otras tres igual.

questions.stem: Which question is NOT a statistical question?
choices: How many home runs did each player hit this year?
How many miles does each runner train per week?
How many innings are in a baseball game?
How tall is each player on the basketball team?
questions.explanation: "How many innings are in a baseball game?" has one fixed answer (9) — no variability. The other questions all produce different answers for different people.
choiceFeedback: Each player hit a different number of home runs—would the answer vary?
Different runners train different miles—would the data vary?
Each player has a different height—would the answers vary?
hints: Careful — this asks for the question that is NOT statistical: the one with a single fixed answer instead of varying data.
For each choice ask: 'Would each player or runner give a different number?' The odd one out is a rule of the game, not data you collect.
Start with 'How tall is each player?' — heights differ player to player, so that one IS statistical. Keep testing until one has just one answer.
questions.stemEs: ¿Cuál pregunta NO es una pregunta estadística?
questions.explanationEs: «¿Cuántas entradas tiene un partido de béisbol?» tiene una sola respuesta fija (9): no hay variabilidad. Las otras preguntas dan respuestas distintas para distintas personas.
choicesEs: ¿Cuántos jonrones bateó cada jugador este año?
¿Cuántas millas entrena cada corredor por semana?
¿Cuántas entradas tiene un partido de béisbol?
¿Cuánto mide cada jugador del equipo de baloncesto?
hintsEs: Cuidado: se pide la pregunta que NO es estadística, la que tiene una sola respuesta fija en lugar de datos que varían.
En cada opción pregunta: '¿daría cada jugador o corredor un número distinto?' La que sobra es una regla del juego, no datos que recolectas.
Empieza con '¿Cuánto mide cada jugador?': las estaturas cambian de jugador a jugador, así que esa SÍ es estadística. Sigue probando hasta hallar una con una sola respuesta.

questions.stem: Why is 'How many hours of sleep did each student get last night?' a statistical question?
choices: Because different students got different amounts of sleep
Because it asks about sleep
Because hours are numbers
Because the answer is always 8 hours
questions.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability — different students slept different amounts, so the data will vary.
choiceFeedback: Sleep is a topic, not why it's statistical—which choice describes variability?
Hours are numbers, but are they used only in statistical questions?
If everyone slept 8 hours, would this be a statistical question?
hints: The question asks WHY it's statistical — focus on what happens when many students answer, not on the topic of sleep.
Think: if you asked every student how long they slept, would you get one number or many different numbers? That idea is called variability.
Picture asking 5 classmates their sleep hours and listing the numbers. Notice whether the list is all the same or varied — that's the key idea.
questions.stemEs: ¿Por qué «¿Cuántas horas durmió cada estudiante anoche?» es una pregunta estadística?
questions.explanationEs: Una pregunta estadística anticipa variabilidad: distintos estudiantes durmieron cantidades distintas, así que los datos van a variar.
choicesEs: Porque distintos estudiantes durmieron cantidades distintas
Porque pregunta sobre el sueño
Porque las horas son números
Porque la respuesta siempre es 8 horas
hintsEs: La pregunta es POR QUÉ es estadística: concéntrate en lo que pasa cuando muchos estudiantes responden, no en el tema del sueño.
Piensa: si le preguntaras a cada estudiante cuánto durmió, ¿obtendrías un número o muchos números distintos? Esa idea se llama variabilidad.
Imagina preguntar a 5 compañeros sus horas de sueño y anotar los números. Fíjate si la lista es toda igual o variada: esa es la idea clave.

steps: 1. Statistical Question: Expects answers that vary across people, trials, or items
2. Non-Statistical Question: Has one single fixed answer
3. Data Collection: Gather varied data points to create a distribution
reviewHighlights.watchOut: A common mistake in Statistical Questions and Data is judging a question by its topic or its numbers instead of its variability. Students see a question about ONE player, ONE game, or ONE fixed fact — like "How many points does the team need to win a game?" — and call it statistical just because it has a number or is about sports. Or they see a question about a single player's whole season, like "How many touchdowns did the quarterback throw this season?", and call it NOT statistical because only one player is named, forgetting that a season covers many games with a different result each time. Both errors skip the real test: will the answers actually differ from case to case (game to game, player to player)? If yes, it is a statistical question; if there is one fixed answer, it is not.

level1.stem: Is this a statistical question? "What is each student's favorite fruit?" Type yes or no.

level1.stem: A soccer team has 11 players on the field. Is "How many players does one team have on the field?" a statistical question? Type yes or no.

level2.explanationEs: Cuenta las respuestas posibles: una respuesta fija: 31 días Decide: sin variación → no es estadística

level2.stem: Is this a statistical question? "How many brothers and sisters does each student in our class have?" Type yes or no.

level2.stem: Which question is NOT statistical? A: "How many pages does each book on this shelf have?" B: "How many pages does this book have?" Type A or B.

level2.explanationEs: Revisa la pregunta A: cada libro → muchas cantidades de páginas Revisa la pregunta B: este libro → una sola cantidad de páginas

level2.stem: A science class studies the weather. Which question is a statistical question?
level2.stemEs: Una clase de ciencias estudia el tiempo. ¿Cuál pregunta es una pregunta estadística?
hints: Look for the question that gives many different answers.
hintsEs: Busca la pregunta que da muchas respuestas distintas.
level2.explanation: Look for the words "each day.": each day in May → many temperatures Check that the answers vary: different temperatures → statistical
level2.explanationEs: Busca las palabras «cada día»: cada día de mayo → muchas temperaturas Revisa que las respuestas varíen: temperaturas distintas → estadística
choices: What is the temperature at noon each day in May?
What was the temperature at noon on May 1?
How many days are in May?
At what temperature does water freeze?
choicesEs: ¿Cuál es la temperatura al mediodía cada día de mayo?
¿Cuál fue la temperatura al mediodía el 1 de mayo?
¿Cuántos días tiene mayo?
¿A qué temperatura se congela el agua?
choiceFeedback: This asks about one day at one time. It has one answer.
May always has the same number of days. That is one fixed answer.
Water freezes at one temperature. That is a fact, not data that varies.

level3.stem: Which question is a STATISTICAL question?
choices: How many minutes did I sleep last night?
How many students are in our class?
What time does school start?
How many minutes did each student in our class sleep last night?
choiceFeedback: This asks about one person, so it has exactly one answer. A statistical question anticipates answers that vary across a group.
A class has one size, so this has a single answer. Statistical questions expect the answers to differ.
School starts at one fixed time, so there is nothing to vary. Ask something that would give different answers from different students.
level3.explanation: A statistical question anticipates answers that VARY. Different students slept different amounts, so the data will vary. The other three each have exactly one fixed answer.

level3.stem: Raj says "How many students are in our class?" is statistical because it is about many students. Is Raj right? Type yes or no.
level3.stemEs: Raj dice que «¿Cuántos estudiantes hay en nuestra clase?» es estadística porque es sobre muchos estudiantes. ¿Tiene razón Raj? Escribe sí o no.
hints: Many students are in the question. But how many answers can it have?
hintsEs: Hay muchos estudiantes en la pregunta. Pero ¿cuántas respuestas puede tener?
level3.explanation: Count the possible answers: one count for the whole class Decide: one fixed answer → not statistical
level3.explanationEs: Cuenta las respuestas posibles: un solo conteo para toda la clase Decide: una respuesta fija → no es estadística

level3.stem: Is this a statistical question? "How many text messages does Omar send each day this month?" Type yes or no.
level3.stemEs: ¿Es esta una pregunta estadística? «¿Cuántos mensajes de texto envía Omar cada día de este mes?» Escribe sí o no.

hintsEs: Busca las palabras «cada día». ¿Variarán las respuestas?

level3.explanationEs: Busca de quién trata la pregunta: 1 persona, muchos días Revisa si las respuestas varían: conteos distintos → estadística

level3.stem: A pet store owner writes four questions. Which one is a statistical question?

hintsEs: Busca la pregunta en la que cada respuesta puede ser distinta.

choices: How much does each puppy in the store weigh?
How many puppies are in the store today?
How much did the store's oldest puppy weigh this morning?
How many legs does a puppy have?

¿Cuántos cachorros hay hoy en la tienda?
¿Cuánto pesó esta mañana el cachorro más viejo de la tienda?

level3.stem: Mr. Ruiz asks, "How many pets does each student have?" Four students all answer 1. Is it still a statistical question?
level3.stemEs: El Sr. Ruiz pregunta: «¿Cuántas mascotas tiene cada estudiante?» Cuatro estudiantes responden 1. ¿Sigue siendo una pregunta estadística?

hintsEs: Una pregunta estadística espera respuestas que varían. Piensa en lo que esperas antes de preguntar.
level3.explanation: Ask: could other students answer differently?: 0, 1, 2, 3 pets are all possible Decide: you expect variety → statistical
level3.explanationEs: Pregunta: ¿podrían otros estudiantes responder distinto?: 0, 1, 2, 3 mascotas son posibles Decide: esperas variación → estadística
choices: Yes. Before you ask, you expect the answers to vary.
No. All the answers were the same.
No. It is about students, not numbers.
Yes. Four students answered.
choicesEs: Sí. Antes de preguntar, esperas que las respuestas varíen.
No. Todas las respuestas fueron iguales.
No. Es sobre estudiantes, no sobre números.
Sí. Respondieron cuatro estudiantes.
choiceFeedback: The test is what you expect before you ask. Other students could answer 0 or 3.
The answers are numbers of pets. Questions about people can give numbers that vary.
Four answers are not enough on their own. The reason is that you expect the answers to vary.

steps.title: Check: does it anticipate variability?
steps.say: Different students should give different answers.

steps.title: Write strong survey questions

items: Pick a new item: pizza, tacos, salad bar, stir-fry

steps.math: answers vary and can be tallied

steps.title: Leave out non-statistical questions

items: How many days a week is lunch served?
same answer for everyone → leave out

steps.math: one fixed answer → not on the survey

workedSteps.answer: Ask questions with varied answers, like a 1–5 rating or a choice of new item (e.g., 45 ÷ 80 = 56.25% pick tacos); leave out one-answer questions.
